extracted.intended_audience: writers, aspiring authors, writing mentors, and members of writing communities
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical standards for paying it forward in the writing field: how to mentor one-on-one, build community structures, and give useful, up-to-date help to other writers. Includes pitfalls to avoid and concrete examples of activities that teach publishing skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share what you have learned / pay it forward
rubrics_metrics.description: Helping one another out, sharing information, share what you have learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be generous with knowledge and experience; give colleagues practical tips and warnings so they avoid the mistakes you made. Examples: Superstars writing seminar origins—colleagues sharing business, contracts, and copyright knowledge. Anti-pattern: hoarding information or only mentoring for personal gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster community and build structures
rubrics_metrics.description: One-on-one mentoring, and fostering a community. Forming friendships within structures. Find your tribe!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create conferences, seminars, magazines, or degree programs that convene cohorts (e.g., Goblin Fruit magazine, Superstars, a publishing MA). Building structures lets people 'ping off' one another and spawn further projects. Guidance: focus on enabling connections, not just delivering content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide one-on-one, targeted mentoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct, individualized mentorship—spot the problem and give the specific fix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for teachable moments and offer concrete, actionable advice (Howard/Lar deSouza example: hand someone a different pen and show how to hold it). These interventions need not be permanent relationships; short focused help can produce big gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and support peer cohorts (find your tribe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find writers who are at your level of writing and help each other out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage cohorts and peer groups where emerging writers support one another; retreats and seminars often produce long-lasting writing groups and networking. Emphasize lateral support rather than top-down instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat people as peers / equal
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentors should approach rising writers as equals where appropriate—this fosters mutual respect, encourages honest exchange, and prevents hierarchical stasis. Example: Kevin treating Dan as an equal at a signing rather than as a student.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep advice current / acknowledge landscape changes
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the pitfalls of mentoring is that the rules change every week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that how you broke in may not apply now. Update your guidance frequently and be explicit about time-bound relevance. Share new developments (e.g., Kindle Unlimited changes) with mentees; avoid presenting outdated tactics as universal truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize practical, hands-on training
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach practical stuff and do hands-on things so that they can actually do it when they have a degree/experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide real-world tasks: running an anthology (solicitations, slush pile reading, contracts, copyediting, cover design, layout, release). Example: Western Colorado University MA students edited a professional anthology to learn the publishing pipeline. Scoring note: prioritize experiential outcomes over abstract lectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach realistic expectations about submissions and slush piles
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers must learn what they’re up against in the slush pile; presentation matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey pragmatic rules: initial-read decisions often happen in a paragraph or less; typos on the first page hurt; a polite cover letter can put you in the top tier. Use examples from students who sifted 535 submissions to illustrate selection realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer flexible, permeable mentoring relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: A mentor relationship doesn’t need to be permanent; it can be permeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to short-term, situational, or lateral mentoring rather than assuming long-term hierarchical mentorship is the only model. Encourage episodic help and peer-based guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give specific, actionable fixes instead of generalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for those moments where you can see the exact problem and offer a concise fix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, targeted advice (e.g., change the tool or tweak a technique) often has outsized impact. Mentors should watch how a writer works to diagnose concrete issues and recommend immediate, testable changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share timely industry updates and practical intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: If you hear about something new that changed on Kindle Unlimited, then share it with other people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act as an information conduit for evolving rules, distribution channels, and business practices. Prompt sharing keeps communities adaptive and informed; rely on networks and podcasts to disseminate changes weekly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage gratitude and acknowledgement of past mentors
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the people who have helped you, and how. Thank them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice the habit-building exercise: list influential people, note what they did, and send a thank-you note. This reinforces networks, models appreciative behavior, and sustains mentor energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize mentorship is reciprocal and prevents calcification
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking mentors questions helps them too — it keeps them from calcifying in their approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame mentorship as mutual learning: mentee questions can reveal changing realities and force mentors to articulate and update methods. This reciprocity is a benefit to both sides and an argument for treating relationships as two-way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actively scout and elevate rising talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Be on the lookout for rising talent and treat them as equals rather than students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentors should pay attention at signings, workshops, and events to spot emerging writers and make introductions or offer opportunities. Being proactive about elevating others strengthens the community and 'lifts all boats.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mentoring with expectation of reward or credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentoring is often not done expecting thanks or credit; don’t make mentorship transactional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentor from generosity rather than expectation. Anti-patterns include mentoring primarily for reputation, reciprocal obligations, or explicit returns; explicit advice: do not condition help on recognition.
